problem: LLM-based behavior-tree (BT) generators for robots mostly depend on closed-source or large API models (GPT-series) that cannot run on robot hardware or offline. Their outputs are often not ROS2/BehaviorTree.CPP-compatible, and there is no standardized benchmark for evaluating LLM-generated BTs. The predecessor, BTGenBot (7B), was slow, hallucinated actions and needed examples.
motivation: BTs from the BehaviorTree.CPP library are the de facto task representation in ROS2 (Nav2), so a local, open, lightweight generator of directly executable BTs would be plug-and-play for real robots. The authors observe that a small, high-quality, real-world-seeded dataset can fine-tune a 1B model to beat frontier LLMs on this narrow task. They also observe that the BT structure itself (Fallback/Retry, blackboard) naturally supports inference-time and runtime error recovery.
key_idea: QLoRA-fine-tune Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on 5,204 synthetic BT/description pairs bootstrapped (via gpt-4o-mini) from 570 real-world-validated BTs, so that it maps (task description + action-primitive list) directly to BehaviorTree.CPP XML. Wrap it with a closed-vocabulary inference validator and a runtime logger that triggers subtree regeneration.
insight: Domain data quality and scale matter more than model size for structured BT generation. The data-scaling ablation (Fig. data scaling) shows ROUGE/BLEU rising monotonically from 46.2/27.4 (600 BTGenBot-style samples) to 82.2/74.8 (5,204 samples), with the biggest jump at 1,413 samples. Supplying the action-primitive list in the input plus a closed-vocabulary validator yields 100% action coherency and XML validity, whereas BTGenBot, trained without action lists, is only 63.46% action-coherent zero-shot. The error-recovery (ER) module is model-agnostic and helps most on hard OOD tasks: BTGenBot-2 goes 84.61→90.38% zero-shot and 92.38→98.07% one-shot. Claude Opus 4.1 goes 65.38→76.92% zero-shot (hard 4/16→7/16), and a single regeneration iteration usually suffices.
method: Dataset curation: 594 TSE real-robot BTs are cleaned to 570 via an XML/BehaviorTree.CPP parser. gpt-4o-mini generates 3 variants per BT with nucleus sampling (top-p 0.99), keeping execution nodes fixed (1,413 BTs). A second round adds 3,791 more, giving 5,204 BTs (~3.5M tokens), each paired with a <200-word task description and an action/parameter list in Alpaca instruction/input/output format.

Model and fine-tuning: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (8k context) is trained with QLoRA on attention (q/k/v/o) and MLP (gate/up/down) projections. Training uses 5 epochs, LR 1e-4, warmup ratio 0.1, batch 16 and a 95/5 train/test split, taking ~30 h on 2× Quadro RTX 6000. The objective maximizes log P(T | instruction, action set).

Inference-time validator: constrains decoding to XML and uses a Python BT parser with a YAML whitelist of allowed control nodes and action primitives. Malformed or hallucinated-action outputs are rejected and regenerated.

Runtime validator: an in-process C++ logger in every tree node records the stack trace and a blackboard snapshot on Failure. If local recovery (Fallback/Retry) does not handle a failure that will propagate, the system requests an LLM subtree regeneration, validates it, and splices it into the tree.

BT Benchmark: 52 BehaviorTree.CPP tasks in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Navigation has 32 tasks (12 easy / 10 medium / 10 hard) and tabletop manipulation has 20 (6/8/6). Hard tasks are intentionally OOD, with novel primitives, fault recovery and conditional logic. Evaluation uses functional metrics (SR, Pass@k, inference time) and non-functional ones (action coherency, XML syntax, human-judged semantic correctness).

numbers_note: Not a standard embodied-navigation benchmark: evaluation is on the authors' own 52-task BT benchmark in Isaac Sim, with no standard nav metrics. Per-level SR and Pass@3 are printed as fractions (e.g. '18 / 18'), stored here as numerator counts with the denominator in the key name. Per-model ROUGE-1/2/L/Lsum/BLEU on the 250-BT test set are only shown in a figure without numeric values. The one-shot BTGenBot-2 Avg SR is printed as 92.38%, but the per-level counts give 48/52 = 92.31%.
results: On the 52-task Isaac Sim BT benchmark, BTGenBot-2-ER reaches 90.38% average SR zero-shot and 98.07% one-shot; without error recovery the figures are 84.61% and 92.38%. The strongest zero-shot baseline, GPT-5 Thinking, gets 71.15%, and one-shot Claude Opus 4.1-ER gets 88.46%. The predecessor BTGenBot reaches 57.69% / 71.15%. The gap is largest on the hard OOD tasks (zero-shot 12/16 vs 5/16 for GPT-5). BTGenBot-2 also generates a BT in ~11 s on a GTX 1080, up to 16× faster than BTGenBot, and achieves 100% action coherency.
limitations: The model has no perception or grounding: it relies on a user-supplied list of predefined action primitives, and task success depends on those primitives. Semantic correctness is judged by only 3 human experts.

The benchmark is self-designed and small (52 tasks, single run per task for SR). Real-robot validation covers only the 18 easy tasks, and there is no comparison with other BT generators (LLM-BT, BETR-XP-LLM, etc.) beyond BTGenBot and general LLMs.

The training data is mostly synthetic (gpt-4o-mini-generated), with quality checked only by visual inspection of a subset. It is about an order of magnitude below the token heuristic for the model size.
